5. RESULTS

The proposed quasi-2-D model has to be validated by comparison with experimental data. However, due to the lack of detailed and reproducible experimental
data of HARCC in the open literature (e.g. [26]), the comparison with validated
CFD solutions can also be considered as an effective validation method. In fact,
CFD solutions provide detailed data in terms of bulk and local variables in the channel cross-section. Moreover, the relatively simple geometry of the test cases (that is,
straight channels) enables focus on the validation of the proposed model rather than
of the semi-empirical relations that supply it. Therefore, two sets of computations
are discussed. The first one is relevant to straight channels validated by comparison
with reference solutions obtained with the CFD solver presented in references [24,
28], which in turn has been validated against the experimental data of heated tubes
in references [24,31]. The second set of computations is relevant to a rocket engine
cooling system, which allows one to demonstrate model capabilities and to validate
results by comparison with gross experimental data.

5.1. Straight Channels

The first validation test case addresses the supercritical methane turbulent flow
in straight channels with asymmetric heating. The reference CFD solutions have been
partially presented in reference [23] and refer to channels with the same length and
cross-section area, but different aspect ratio of the cross-section: 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16,
respectively. The dimensions of the channels are shown in Table 1 and the boundary
conditions are as follows. The methane inlet stagnation temperature is 220 K and the
stagnation pressure is 90 bar, while the back pressure at the channel exit is 70 bar. The
channel wall is smooth and the imposed wall temperature ranges from 600 K at the
bottom wall (y ¼ 0) to 220 K at the top wall (y ¼ h). A linear wall temperature distribution is imposed on the side wall to simulate the fin effect. The supercritical methane
behavior is described by means of the MBWR equation of state [34].

The typical temperature flow-fields obtained by CFD computations are presented for two configurations in Figure 3 at various cross-sections, from the inlet
toward the exit. The first geometric configuration (k ¼ 1), represents the limit case
of the low aspect ratio cooling channel (that is, square section), whereas the second

high-density, low-temperature state at 220 K. It is heated up by the entering heat flux
from the hot walls and thus the coolant temperature distribution in a channel
cross-section is strongly stratified. At the last channel section, the temperature stratification almost reproduces the imposed wall temperature distribution. This is particularly evident in the case of a high aspect ratio (Figure 3b).

To reproduce the described methane flow-fields, the coolant inlet conditions of
the quasi-2-D model are the same mass flow rate and inlet static temperature and
pressure of the CFD solutions. The boundary conditions for the quasi-2-D model
are those of imposed wall temperature. The coefficients fw and hw are computed
according to Petukhov’s semiempirical relations [35], which apply to straight,
smooth channel flow, and present good accuracy in the case of supercritical fluids
(that is, far enough from the critical region) for a wide range of Reynolds number
(from 10 <sup>4</sup> to 5 � 10 <sup>6</sup> ). The semiempirical relations for the skin friction are
